maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-UNEMPLOYMENT RULING OP MR. SPEAKER ON AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS
speechtext:
Last evening shortly before adjournment a question of order was raised on which I reserved my decision, and said I would give it today at three o'clock.
The motion is that the Speaker leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of ways and means. To this an amendment is moved by Mr. Heaps as follows:
In the opinion of this house it is desirable that a committee or commission be appointed to consider the economic situation in the dominion with special reference to unemployment and to report back during the present session of parliament.
A point of order has been raised that the amendment is out of order on the ground that it again introduces a matter that was debated and disposed of when the right hon. the leader of the opposition moved as part of an amendment to the address:
The house regrets that, except the dole, the government has no policy with respect to the relief of unemployment.
I have carefully considered the arguments presented on the question of order, examined the authorities and precedents of both the British and Canadian houses of parliament. In the debate on the amendment of the right hon. leader of the opposition to the address I find that he suggested that a committee or commission be appointed and given charge of the whole question of unemployment relief, which shows that the subject matter of the proposed amendment was then open to dis-
*1420	COMMONS

cussion and actually debated. If this amendment is allowed it inevitably follows that there will be a repetition of the debate on unemployment.
The ordinary rules of debate are applicable on this occasion; for instance, a matter already decided by the house cannot be discussed. See Bourinot at page 420.
This amendment is offered on the motion to go into committee of ways and means, and not being accepted by the government is a motion of want of confidence, and the fact that it provides for the appointment of a commission or committee with special reference to unemployment is in effect a condemnation of the government's policy on that question.
The house has refused to condemn the government's policy on unemployment by rejecting the amendment moved to the address by the leader of the opposition. In view of that decision by the house I cannot find that this amendment, being a motion of want of confidence dealing, also with unemployment, is in order.

Is it the pleasure of the house that the Speaker's decision be sustained?

speechtext: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the third reading of Bill No. 4, respecting a certain trade agreement between the Dominion of Canada and the Irish Free State.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE IRISH FREE STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will recall that when this bill was before us in its previous stages, the government conceded that it did not involve any increase in duties; that as a matter of fact it secured to Canadian merchandise in the Irish market as favourable treatment as would be accorded to that of any other country and vice versa. We have been contending all along that any agreement that was made should not in any

particular deprive our country of extending, if we so desired, favourable treatment to any other country that wished to trade with us, and as the legislation in this respect is along the lines that we have been advocating I imagine that most on this side will be prepared to support it.
It has another feature which entirely distinguishes it from the agreement arrived at with South Africa or the proposed agreement with the United Kingdom, namely, that it does not involve any increase of duty nor has it that moist objectionable of all features, the fixing of a margin of preference for a period of years, thereby depriving this country of the opportunity of according to any other countries that may wish to trade with us as favourable treatment as we are according in this case. There is a great distinction, Mr. Speaker, between certain of these agreements and the agreement which is proposed with South Africa and the agreement which is proposed with the United Kingdom. These differences were pointed out at the time the agreement with Rhodesia and the agreement with Ireland were before the house, and as hon. members will recall, there was for that reason no opposition to either the agreement with Rhodesia or the agreement with Ireland at the time these measures were discussed on the first and second readings and in committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE IRISH FREE STATE
TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE IRISH FREE STATE
speechtext:
That is the last word, I presume, Mr. Speaker, coming from the hon. gentleman.
The house will recall that week after week and day after day for the last six or seven weeks the right hon. leader of the opposition has been reiterating to the point of becoming tedious his objection to the five-year provision. Now he acquiesces in this. This is quite all right, he says, and we are all going to vote for it. He virtually invites no division, and instructs his followers to line up behind this bill, after he has kept the house for about six weeks arguing on the question. He says that this is a marked advance upon the British agreement.

Irish Free State
Now this hill gives to Ireland, so far as entry into this market is concerned, precisely what we give to Great Britain. To give to Great Britain certain concessions in this, that and the other sort of article is a vicious principle in the way we have done it; but to give it to Ireland, the right hon. gentleman says, is perfectly all right and all my followers should vote for it. AVhat does article 2 of this trade agreement say? It says:
Goods, the produce or manufacture of the Irish Free State, imported into Canada, shall not be subject to other or higher duties than those paid on similar goods, the produce or manufacture of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
This whole bill is based upon, allied to, intertwined and amalgamated with, or any other similar term you like to use, the British agreement. Every jot and tittle, every crossed t and every dotted i, of the British agreement is in this, and yet the right hon. gentleman tells us that it is an act of virtue on his part to vote for this agreement, but that the government and all its supporters are doing this country irreparable injury by voting for the British bill. Surely the right hon. gentleman now realizes the spectacle that he has been making before this house and the country for the last six weeks in his protestations and flimsy pretext regarding the five-year period and other provisions of the British bill. This is the British bill simplified into one little clause. All we have done for the British we are doing for the Irish, and all we have done against the British we are doing against the Irish. Any concessions we have given to the British we give to the Irish. The Irish asked for them and got them.
It is not necessary to add anything further. Those are the facts, and we now have the measure of the sincerity of the right hon. gentleman.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE IRISH FREE STATE
speechtext: I am pleased to say, Mr. Speaker, that I am going to vote against the third reading of this bill. It is not at all the same as the Rhodesia bill to which we have just given third reading. In this bill we are granting to the Irish Free State the same terms that are being granted to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. We on this side have been complaining that the tariff has been raised against other countries in order to give a preference on articles coming from Great Britain. The same thing applies to the Irish Free State under section 3 of this bill. There is nothing similar in the treaty with Rhodesia, which was merely a trade agreement in the nature of other trade agreements, and which we accepted as a matter of course.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE IRISH FREE STATE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE IRISH FREE STATE
speechtext: I am sorry if that is beyond the understanding of some hon. gentlemen opposite, but I cannot help that. I am simply giving my own views, and only by looking at the two bills will hon. gentlemen opposite appreciate what the vital distinction is between the two. I am voting against the third reading of this bill.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE IRISH FREE STATE
speechtext:
Before this vote is taken, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I intended, even before the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) spoke, to vote against this bill. My reason for doing so is this: When I read that an Imperial economic conference would be held in Ottawa I presumed from the word "imperial" itself, that it would be a meeting between loyal brethren of the British Empire, but to my surprise I found that the delegates from the Irish Free State who came over to this conference refused to take the oath of allegiance to the King when the government of the Irish Free State was elected. They also refused to pay to the British government a large sum of money due on land annuities which the British government had advanced to the people of Ireland, thereby putting themselves outside the pale of any imperial conference. I therefore say that in my opinion none of the gentlemen representing the Irish Free State had any right to sit either in this chamber or around the economic conference table, nor did Canada have the right to make an agreement with them at an imperial conference. So I am going to vote against the bill.

Yes, I am, I have always been opposed to the principle of imperial unity, for reasons frequently given, in forty years of public life, and of which I am not ashamed; reasons which have received the warmest approval of some of the foremost statesmen and leaders of public thought in

Great. Britain. ' Opposed to imperial unity, I stand with equal frankness for fiiendly cooperation between Great Britain and her sister .nations. In other words, I oppose imperial unity,. so called, because it does not tend to keep the relations between these various communities on the only footing which can preserve them.
With regard to Ireland, Mr. Speaker, my sentiments are well known. I have always been a friend of Ireland, and I have proven it before the war, during the war, and after the war. In days when not one single Irish-Canadian, at least not one that I know in this chamber, would dare to stand by the leaders and principles of Sinn Fein, I did it in public. To trade relations with Ireland I have no objection. To better trade relations with England I have no objection. To better trade relations with South Africa, or any other of the British dominions, I have no objection. But I haA'e objection to all these agreements, because, I repeat, they are based on a principle of policy against which I have fought all my life, and which the greatest leader that the Conservative party has known, Sir John A. Macdonald, opposed all Jus life.

Yes, he did, in word and in deed. When the so-called loyalist people of this country accused him of endangering the British connection because he claimed for the people of Canada the right to the full and unhampered exercise of their economic autonomy, Sir John replied coolly: "so much the worse for British connection." Not that he wanted to break the tie; but he wanted to assert on the part of Canada the same right to exercise her full rights as a nation, as a gOArernment and as a parliament in matters of trade and in matters of taxation as she had won in matters of political management. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to this particular treaty; but not for the reason given by my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff). I heal'd my good friend say that we should not vote for this treaty because of the refusal of Irish members to take the oath of allegiance. That has nothing to do with the matter of this treaty, I will go further. The refusal of the Irish who do not believe in the right of England to rule their country to take the oath of allegiance is a proof of their moral honesty. But I am opposed to this treaty, I am opposed to the preceding treaty, I am opposed to the following treaty, and I will vote against all of them, as I said a few weeks ago, with any group or any party, with any member or

Irish Free State
members of this house, not through any friendship for or antagonism to any country, but in the interests of Canada; because I believe that in the interest of our relations with Great Britain and the other nations we should come back to the sound policy of absolute freedom in matters of trade, and negotiate such treaties as we may choose with any of these countries, whether Great Britain or Ireland or Australia, on the economic merits of the treaties and the trade that can be developed, entirely apart from the principle which governs these agreements, that is, that we must have a series of treaties because we belong to the same empire. No. no; as far as that is concerned I remain faithful to the policy which was propounded, upheld and applied by Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Charles Tupper for twenty years.

TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN : CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the third reading of Bill No. 8, respecting a certain, trade agreement between His Majesty's government in Canada and His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
the,house will recall that when the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. .Bennett) introduced a resolution to approve the trade agreement between the United Kingdom and Canada I took very strong exception to the house proceeding in the manner in which the Prime Minister, said it must proceed. I stated at that, time that I believed the correct procedure was that the house; before being asked to give its approval to'the Canada-United Kingdom agreement, should go into committee of ways and means to consider as a whole and in detail the changes in our tariff which would be necessary in order to give effect to the agreement) and the full significance of these changes. I protested as strongly as I could at the time against our being obliged to proceed with the approval of that particular agreement or any agreement until we had discussed in committee of ways and means the whole of the tariff changes which it involved. I did this on the resolution and I did it again on each of the several stages of the bill up to the present time. We have not had an opportunity of discussing in committee of ways and means the various proposed changes in the tariff, and I wish now to protest again against our being called upon to pass the third reading of a measure, which gives approval to the agreement between the United Kingdom and Canada before we have had opportunity to consider in committee of ways and means the tariff changes involved.
In doing this I wish to support my protest and appeal by bringing to the attention of the house the procedure adopted in the British parliament with respect to these agreements and show wherein the procedure adopted in this House of Commons has been entirely at variance with the British procedure. It has been not only at variance with the British procedure but, according to the statement of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, it has been a procedure which cannot be justified under the British method of proceeding in these matters. Need I say, in this connection, that had the house proceeded in the regular manner some of the misunderstandings which have

United. Kingdom
arisen with respect to these agreements would never have arisen. I now direct attention to what took place in the British parliament with respect to the introduction of these agreements and their consideration. The British parliament considered the agreements first of all on October 18. On that date the house was moved into committee of ways and means to consider the resolutions with respect to imperial preferences, and the discussion occupied October 18, 19 and 20. The resolutions were reported and discussed separately on October 21, 24 and 25. On October 25 a bill with respect to the approval of the agreement for the first time was introduced and given its first reading. It was discussed and given its second reading on October 26 and 27, discussed in committee October 28 and 31, November 1, 2 and 3, and given its third reading on November 3.
I wish to invite the attention of the house particularly to the words of the Chancellor of the Exchequer at the time of moving the house into committee of ways and means in order to consider the resolutions. The house will find the record in Parliamentary Debates of the House of Commons of Great Britain for October 18, 1932. I read from page 37: Orders of the day; ways and means, considered in committee:
Motion made, and question proposed,
"That it is expedient-
(a) to make provision, more especially in connection with the agreements made at the Imperial economic conference held at Ottawa and an announcement made at that conference on behalf of His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom, for imperial preferences, whether as respects the whole or any part of the British Empire, and whether in respect of duties charged under any resolutions of this house having for their object the fulfilment of the agreements aforesaid or duties under the Import Duties Act, 1932, or any other duties-"
There are other provisions:
" (b) to empower the Board of Trade, in the circumstances contemplated in the agreement made between His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom and His Majesty's government in Canada, by order to prohibit the importation of goods of a class or description grown, produced or manufactured in a foreign country;
Paragraph (c) refers to Australia and New Zealand.	'
"(d) for the purpose of giving effect to certain of the provisions of the agreement made between His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom and His Majesty's government in Canada to amend the law with respect to the importation of Canadian cattle;
"(e) to make such other provision as may appear necessary or expedient for the purpose of giving effect to any of the agreements aforesaid."

The Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Chamberlain, then spoke as follows:
I hope that, after all the numerous questions and answers on the subject, there is now no doubt in the minds of the committee as to the procedure which is to be followed. We cannot introduce the bill which is to implement the agreements arrived at at Ottawa until we have obtained from the committee of ways and means the series of resolutions which are on the order paper today.
Nothing could be more specific than that. The Chancellor of the Exchequer said to the British House of Commons that- under its procedure-let me quote his exact words:
We cannot introduce the bill which is to implement the agreements arrived at at Ottawa until we have obtained from the committee of ways and means the series of resolutions which are on the order paper today.
Here, in this House of Commons of Canada, we have had laid on the table resolutions with respect to ways and means intended to provide what is necessary in the way of implementing the agreements, but we have not yet discussed these in detail; we have not had any opportunity to go into committee of ways and means; in fact this house has not even yet adopted a motion to resolve itself into committee of ways and means. Nevertheless we are being asked now to give approval to the third reading of the bill implementing the agreement. Mr. Chamberlain, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, has made it plain that under the procedure of the British parliament it is impossible for the House of Commons to consider the bill before the ways and means committee has taken up the discussion with respect to the tariff changes involved.

If we had had a committee of ways and means to discuss in detail all the tariff changes that were necessary and had we seen as a result of that discussion, the significance of what was being proposed, some of us, particularly myself, would not have been as confused or misled as apparently we have been with respect to the exact meaning of some of the provisions of some of these bills.
Let me complete what Mr. Chamberlain said. He continued:
When I sit down 1 propose to move the first of those resolutions, and I daresay you, Sir Dennis-
That is Sir Dennis Herbert, who was the chairman of the committee:

A little later the chairman of the committee made a statement to the house as to procedure of the committee and as it was agreed upon by all parties in the British House of Commons. The chairman's remarks are reported at page 43 as follows:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
I think, perhaps, before the discussion proceeds, that it may be useful if I oan get the approval, or otherwise, of the committee to the course which I suggest with regard to the debate. I gather from what has taken place at question time that it will probably meet with the approval of the committee. It is that we should follow the same course as was adopted in the case of the resolutions dealing with the Import Duties Act in February last, that is, the course analagous to the budget debates. If the committee approve of that, it will mean that there will be a general discussion on the resolution which has been moved by the Chancellor of the Exchequer; that discussion will range over all the ways and means resolutions which are on the order paper. When the debate comes to an end, all the resolutions will be put one after the other without further debate, leaving the resolutions to be considered separately on the report stage.
I hope that that will meet with the approval of the committee generally.
Elsewhere the chairman of the committee made special mention of the fact that hon. members would be free to move for the reduction of any duty that appeared in the resolutions which were placed before the house; that it would be entirely in order to move any amendment, and he took great care repeatedly to say that in so doing they had not before them the bill approving the agreement, but that they were free to discuss in the first instance the significance of all items and resolutions so that in the light of them and with full understanding of their significance they might take such action as

they deemed best when asked to pass a bill approving the agreement.
That course has been entirely departed from in this house; it has been departed from knowingly on the part of the government and against the protests and appeals of hon. gentlemen on this side to have the matter correctly proceeded with. I submit that the whole proceeding has been irregular and that it is contrary to British parliamentary practice and also to our own constitution which governs the powers and procedure of this parliament.
Just to show how, as a result of our having proceeded in the manner in which the government has done, some of us have been led astray as to the significance of what was really in the mind of the government, may I draw attention to the sequence in which these measures have been placed before us and to a question which I asked the Prime Minister when we were discussing the trade agreement between Canada and Rhodesia? This is reported in Hansard at page 892, as follows:
Mr. Mackenzie King: May I ask the minister whether in his opinion the net result of the agreement is that as a result of the tariff changes tariffs will really be lowered as against Rhodesia?
Mr. Bennett:	The answer is found in the
fact that the goods come in free. I would think it would be difficult to say, but in my judgment the effect would be probably to lower the tariff.
Having consistently taken the view that whatever would help to lower tariffs as between different parts of the British Empire was desirable, I for one, when that measure was before the house, gave it support not only on the second reading, but again this afternoon on the third. When the Irish agreement was before us, may I point out that we had not then had before us the British agreement. We were presented with the bill with respect to the approval of the agreement between the Irish Free State and Canada immediately after the bill respecting Rhodesia and before the bills respecting South Africa and the United Kingdom, and in reading that bill I would challenge anyone to place upon it an interpretation other than the one which we placed upon it at the time and which I believe the text will bear out as the one reasonable interpretation to be placed upon it, namely, that whatever we might do for Britain we would do equally by wray of favourable treatment to Ireland. In other words, while the present administration is in office, if it intends to deal with Britain along the lines of the present agreement, then it is com-

United Kingdom
mitted to extending the same kind of treatment to Ireland. On the other hand, should there be a change of government and a Liberal administration come into office, which were to decide that it was not going to continue the British agreement and obtained the consent of the British government to changes in the agreement in any or many particulars, we would be obliged under the Irish-Canadian agreement to give the same treatment to Ireland as we gave to Britain. That is the view I have had all along as to the significance of the Irish agreement, and it is the only view, it seems to me, that one reading the bill by itself could take in the light of the phraseology of the measure itself. I know, of course, that the side notes and memoranda attached to bills toy the government are not part of the bill itself, but they are all intended as guides to parliament. Looking at this trade agreement, which has only five sections, the first approves of the trade agreement, and anyone looking at the terms of the trade agreement will see nothing there that could be objectionable reading it in the light of what I have just said. Clause 3, which is the one to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has just referred, has the following opposite it in the margin: "Extension of advantage to Irish Free State," that is, extension to the Irish Free State of the advantage of what would be given to Britain. That seems to me a perfectly fair and just attitude for Canada to take towards Ireland. But had I understood at the time or had I ever had the slightest idea that in being asked to extend to Ireland treatment equal to that which we are extending to Britain we were thereby obliging ourselves to raise and maintain duties against other countries, I certainly would not for one moment have countenanced that particular clause or the bill which contains it.
May I ask, Mr. Speaker, if it is the desire and design of the government in dealing with these imperial agreements to trick us into some adherence or agreement to a measure? Is there a motive-in all of this so sinister that the administration itself is not perfectly frank with parliament in regard to the full meaning and significance of these measures? I say that if the government had been straightforward in this matter and had presented to parliament in the first instance, as the British government did, their resolutions to be considered in committee of ways and means, and after discussing the British agreement we had taken up these other agreements which the government now says are based on the British agreement, instead of taking up the other agreements first before we had even con-53719-911
sidered the significance of the British agreement, there would have been no danger of misunderstanding. Such misunderstanding as has arisen has arisen from that source. It bears out very strongly, I think, what I said on a previous occasion, and to which some-exception was then taken, that it looks to me very much as if there was a conspiracy in this matter somewhere on the part of some of those who had to do with the making of these agreements. Hon. gentlemen opposite have taken exception to the words "Tory conspiracy," but may I say that to my mind high protection and Toryism are synonymous, and I believe that there has been in the minds of the Prime Minister and others of his administration an effort, under the guise of these trade agreements, to appeal, on the one hand, to the patriotism of the people of the country and, on the other, by a subterfuge, to put across tariffs which will increase the already inordinately high tariffs of this country, and which will make a large part of our tariff schedules permanent for a number of years.
If it is the unity of the empire amongst other things that we are considering, I think it is most unfortunate indeed that in our own parliament we could not have complete frankness on the part of the administration as to the exact purport of agreements proposed and that we should not be accorded the same rights and privileges as are accorded to the members of the British House of Commons. I protest very strongly, Mr. Speaker, against Canadian members of parliament not being accorded the same rights and privileges as members of the British House of Commons. These rights and privileges have been denied to us, and I say again most emphatically that if that were the only ground upon which we could ask the members of the house to oppose the agreement at this stage it would be an amply sufficient ground.
I am not going to go over again the many reasons why we oppose the Canada-United Kingdom agreement, for they have already been amply stressed. But what has taken place this afternoon has brought out a new feature which makes those reasons stronger than ever, and I am very glad that it has, because it makes clearer than ever the reason why we should oppose not only the United Kingdom agreement but the other agreements as well. It has been made perfectly clear here this afternoon that what is intended is not what we were led to believe, a series of bilateral agreements between Canada and other parts of the empire, each of which stood on its own feet, and was to be read only in the

light of what appeared on the face of it, but rather by means of clauses and schedules referring to what is part of some other bill, an effort so to entangle the whole tariff structure of the British Empire that hereafter it will become impossible for independent action to be taken on the part of the parliament of Canada with respect to most of its own tariff, an effort effectively to restrict its freedom in respect of fiscal matters all along the line. All this bears out what the Prime Minister said, that really what we are doing here is not to follow any national policy with respect to the tariff in Canada, but that we are in the midst of framing an imperial tariff policy which will so bind this country in the years to come that it will be impossible for our tariff as it stands to be modified in any particular, seeing that either as respect Africa or Rhodesia or Australia or New Zealand or Newfoundland or the Irish Free State or the United Kingdom itself something will be found in the agreements which will make it impossible to make changes which may be vastly in the public interest without violating in some way the unity of empire or bringing in question our loyalty to the empire, and all the rest of it.
I want to say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that so far as the procedure is concerned, this House of Commons having been obliged to depart from British procedure, you yourself as Speaker should rule that the procedure up to the present has been wholly out of order and not in accordance with British parliamentary practice, and then permit us to reconsider these agreements in accordance with the full rights and privileges of a British parliament.

speechtext:
I am not going to touch upon the question of procedure. The Minister of Finance, from his point of view, has made it quite clear that the procedure followed was according to the rules of our house, whether good or bad. In some respects we should follow closely what is done in England, because the English have a longer and wider experience of parliamentary procedure than we have. On the other hand I agree fully and unreservedly with the Minister of Finance when he says that if there is anything wrong in our rules, we should change them according to our needs.
But there is one point that I wish to bring up at this moment, before we pass on to the third reading. My objection to all these treaties-including the Southern Rhodesia treaty, against which I voted, as against all the others-is the objection which was so eloquently expressed by the right hon. leader of the opposition, and not eloquently but with conviction, so far as I am concerned, by myself: that these treaties put impediments in the way of our world trade. That is my main reason, and I stick to it. With regard to the English treaty, I did not take any part in the discussion in committee; I left it to better informed members of the house to take up the various items and argue pro and con. The debate was extremely interesting and illuminating, although somewhat protracted. But the point I want to make now is the same I made previously: impediments in our foreign trade; and I take as an example our possible relations with France.
During the debate in committee, one hon. member to my left pointed out that as regarded a certain item of the tariff, we were making it more difficult to trade with Holland. I now wish to point out that in this treaty we are making it more difficult, by various changes in the tariff and by the fixation of duty on certain articles for five years, to make a good treaty with France. I understand from press reports Jhat my excellent personal friend-if I may call him so without compromising him in the eyes of some of the supporters of the government-the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan), is now in Paris endeavouring to negotiate a treaty with the French government. No gentleman in this house and no member of the government is better qualified to carry on such negotiations; but without intending to embarrass the hon.

gentleman I should like to point out some of the provisions of this treaty which will make it more difficult for him to conclude a bargain good for Canada as well as for France.
At the outset may I say that I discard entirely the sentimental aspect, so far as French Canada is concerned; though it would be just as legitimate for the French Canadians to desire to make trade arrangements with France on a basis of sentiment as it is legitimate for Canadians of English or Scotch origin to desire trade arrangements with British countries on that basis. I will endeavour to remain true to myself. When I first ran for the House of Commons, in 1896, a trade agreement had just been concluded between Canada and France. The negotiations were carried on by Sir George Foster, then Mr. Foster, a minister of the Conservative administration in Canada, and by M. Jules Siegfried, Minister of Commerce of France. The Conservative candidates in the province of Quebec boasted that the Conservative government having made the first trade arrangement with France, our former motherland, we therefore should vote for the Conservative party. I took the ground that all trade arrangements whether with France, England or any other country on earth, should be judged from the viewpoint of Canadian interests. That is still my position. Let me add, however, that though sentiment should not be the inspiration of a trade agreement; though business considerations and economic principles should be the two guiding thoughts in the minds or those representing any country negotiating with another country, it must be acknowledged, that even in trade arrangements, there are what Bismarck called imponderable considerations which must be taken into account.
Now let us face the facts as they really are. Whether or not some of us like it, the fact remains that one-fourth the population of Canada is French by origin and French in culture; that they read French books and magazines; that, as pointed out the other day by the hon. member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset), their physicians go to Paris to finish their studies and come back with notions of French science; they are familiar with the French pharmacopoeia; they make use of French surgical instruments and recommend to their patients the use of French remedies, which are counted among t.he best, and which have the great advantage over our own that you can read upon the bottle or box what is contained in the medicine prescribed by your doctor. Now I take this treaty, and when I

United Kingdom
read through the items what do I find? Here is item 171, covering books. It carries a duty of "free" under the British preference, 10 per cent under the intermediate tariff and 10 per cent under the general tariff. Then item 206, covering serums; this is free under the British preference, 20 per cent under the intermediate tariff and 20 per cent under the general tariff. Item 229 deals with common or laundry soap, and the duty per one hundred pounds is 50 cents under the British preference and SI .50 under the intermediate and general tariffs. Then we come to castile soap, most of which is manufactured at Marseille. The duty per pound is free under the British preference and 2 cents under the intermediate and general tariffs. Then we have perfumery, a class of goods, as everyone admits, produced par excellence in France. The duty is 20 per cent under the British preferential tariff and 40 per cent under the intermediate and general tariffs. I find manufactures of aluminum carrying a duty of 15 per cent under the British preference and 30 per cent under the intermediate and general tariffs. Then we have kitchen or household utensils of aluminum. Here again anyone who has travelled has found that French-made utensils of this kind are by far the best, the most elegant, among the cheapest and at the same time the most enduring. Under the British preference the duty is 20 per cent, and under the intermediate and general tariffs it is 30 per cent. Then I come to surgical instruments, which were dealt with by the hon. member for Ri-mouski. These are free under the British preference, with a 10 per cent duty under the intermediate and general tariffs. I come to a very important item, that of chemicals and drugs. By excision from item 711 these are now free under the British preference, with a 25 per cent duty under the intermediate and general tariffs.
I have taken at random some of the items in connection with which France is predominant, some of the items our people are accustomed to purchase at the general store, at the chemist's and at the bookstore. These ' articles are imported from France; they form part of our everyday life, part of our culture. A few weeks ago I received a letter from a firm of large importers of French chemicals, in Montreal. Their trade is made up exclusively of importations from France, drugs and chemicals of the highest character and so on. They supply the hospitals of Quebec as well as certain institutions in New Brunswick and in northern and eastern Ontario.
They also import perfumes and goods of that kind. By this treaty we are tying our hands; we are forbidding ourselves the right to offer terms of preferment to France in connection with the exportation of these goods to Canada. Not only are we offering to Great Britain a preference on articles in the manufacture of which the British are inferior to the French; but by reason of the fact that we have raised the intermediate tariff to the level of the general tariff, we are binding ourselves not to offer France a preference on any one of the items I have named as against the rest of the world. We are not able to offer France more favourable terms than we can offer Germany, Italy, Spain or any other country on earth in connection with books, serums, soaps, perfumery, manufactures of aluminum, surgical instruments, chemicals and drugs. I claim that this is unfair to us, not only to French Canada but to Canada generally.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, we French Canadians have a first right in this regard. No one will dispute that it is the right of the French Canadian to purchase French books, to read those French books, to have those French books given his children for their education or their amusement on the same terms that our English speaking friends offer English books to their children. Surely there is not one father of a family in this house who would claim that it is as fair to tax the French father of a large family and make him pay a penalty because his children read French as it is to provide duty free English books for a classical Yankee-Ontario family consisting of father, mother and pet dog. We have families of five, six, eight and ten children, girls going to convent and boys going to college, some in commercial schools and others in classical colleges, all of whose text books are in French. A large proportion of the primers, of course, are printed and published in Canada; but from France we import all the great classics in the French language, a source of pride not only to all people who speak French in any part of the world, but also to all civilized beings-a source of intellectual pride and enjoyment to meh and women everywhere, whether they be of English, Scottish or Irish origin.
After forty years of public life and travel through the various provinces in Canada, I have found, to my delight, in the last ten or fifteen years, a fast-growing knowledge of French in all the English-speaking sections of this country. If there is in my disloyal eyes one redeeming feature about our participation in the nefarious war of 1914-18, it is the growing interest which a large number of

English-Canadians are now taking in French literature and affairs. I might name some of these people like my hon. friend from Toronto South (Mr. Geary), who was an officer in the Canadian army in France. That hon. gentleman learned French there and is now a reader of French books. Occasionally I go to Toronto or Winnipeg, where I find branches of L'AUiance Frangaise, kept up by the enthusiasm and the intellectual interest of university men such as Professor Osborne of Winnipeg, a leading member of Manitoba university. They are consumers of French books and literature. Why do you tax them 10 per cent as against the average Canadian who prefers, as is his right, to read English books because he knows nothing else?
I will go further. From a point of view which I am sure will appeal to the Prime Minister as well as to the leader of the opposition, taking a much broader view than the simple aspect of trade, taking the basic conditions of our country and the necessity of using every means, political, economic, literary and social to build up a strong Canadian nationality, I claim that we must take all legitimate means to preserve this Canada of ours from the insidious and constant penetration of Yankee ideals and literature, and Yankee morals or immorality. I am not saying this against the American nation. There are in the United States plenty of cultured people, and good people, living a moral life. But I must say that the contact between Canada and the United States is made, as a rule, not through such people. Our country is being flooded with the cheapest and commonest American literature. The vast majority of our youth ignore entirely those splendid works of literature and history, of poetry and science, that have their birth in the United States, preferring to purchase the dime novel and that filthy literature that comes by the carload from across the border. We in Quebec are trying, for all we are worth, to preserve the French language in order to safeguard our youth from such contamination.
I appeal to the leaders in this parliament, to whatever party or race they belong: Do you not think that we are doing a service to the whole of Canada in preserving one-fourth of its population from penetration by the ideals of a foreign country? Let us leave aside questions of morality; let us discuss the matter from the national or even the imperial point of view. Does anyone think it makes for the greater loyalty of Canadian people towards England to allow them to Americanize themselves from day to day, from week to week, from year to year? No,

sir. If you want a true Canadian, of whatever race or province or party or religion, to be a bulwark against Americanism, you must cultivate such a Canadian not by making him more British but more Canadian, whether he speaks English or French. As I have said frequently, whether we are of French or English descent, whether we worship in a Catholic or in a Protestant church, there is one and only one sentiment by means of which you can unite the people of Canada, and that is devotion, not to the empire, not to Great Britain, not to France, but to Canada.
Now, Canada is a confederacy of people of varied types; but I do not think it is any disparagement of foreign races such as are represented by some of the most worthy members of this house-Germans, Lithuanians, Hungarians and so forth-to say that after all the history and the mental composition of Canada have had their sources largely in the two races that founded this country-and again I am echoing the words of that man for whom I have cherished all through my political life the greatest admiration, Sir John Macdonald. It was through the free association of the best representatives of the British races and of British culture-whether English, Scottish, Irish or Welsh, it does not matter-and the representatives of French culture and French aspirations, whether of Norman or of Poitevin origin, as my own is, that we created a national soul, composite, dual in its language and diverse in its aspirations. That is the one original characteristic of Canada. It is not our political institutions, half British and half American. It is not our school system-even in Quebec I would not say it is our school system, and certainly it is not the school system throughout the English provinces which have largely adopted the American system of education. It is not our economic life alone, which is but a replica of American economic life. It is not the interchange of trade alone; because, in spite of treaties and tariffs, we still trade more with the United States than with the whole of the British Empire taken together. No. Do not rely only on trade, on dollars and cents, on labour organizations or on , capitalistic institutions to preserve Canada; but draw upon the moral elements of the community and the ethnical aspirations; and even, as I have frequently said, do not disregard the prejudices of the various elements who compose the country. For my part, I have never begrudged the English-Canadian, whether of English or Scottish origin, his devotion to the empire although I dread a little the imperialism of the Irishman. In my

United, Kingdom
youth I had a very good Irish friend, a dear one. He had lived in the United States, in Brazil and elsewhere; he could speak three or four languages, but he had preserved his Irish brogue and his Irish mind. One day, speaking with me about someone else, another Irishman, he said, " Never trust an Irishman	who has	touched	the
king's shilling." There is a good deal of truth in that because, as a rule, the Irishman who has touched the king's shilling has betrayed the country of his birth. Even the king cannot trust him. But in Canada all true Irishmen, all true Scotchmen, all true Englishmen and all French-Canadians, faithful to their origin-at least to the point where it is permissible to be faithful to a foreign country from which one's forefathers have come-agreed some seventy years ago to form a nation. Later on, under the leadership of that great Canadian statesman, Sir John Macdonald, they decided to free their common country from any restriction, legal, political or material, imposed by the British in connection with our fiscal laws. As I stated a moment ago, Sir John Macdonald declared: so much worse for British connection, if the maintenance of British connection means the maintenance of Canadian inferiority. One of his successors, I do not know whether it was Sir John Thompson or Sir Mackenzie Bowell, it does not matter which, entered into a treaty with France. In our trade relations with England we should not forget the necessity of trade with other countries, especially France. On the other hand, in our trade negotiations with France we should not forget the interests which we have at stake in British countries. In all our trading, whether with France, with Great Britain, with Ireland with Southern Rhodesia or any country, our first duty is to the people of Canada.
I appeal to the most generous and enlightened English speaking members of this house. I am sure if they thought seriously of this matter there would be no opposition to my proposal. I repeat, we French Canadians have the right to purchase French books as cheaply as English speaking Canadians can purchase English books; we have the right to purchase chemicals coming from France as cheaply as those which come from Germany or England, and we have the right to purchase aluminum utensils for our households produced in France as cheaply as articles produced in other countries. As far as we are concerned, we feel that this is a matter of right, but there is more than that. The house should consider the advantage to Canada as a whole in enlarging her trade relations, especially with countries with a similarity of tastes and education. This will make for closer and more constant economic relations; it is the sentiment which should be expressed in our economic relations.
One further observation and then I am through.

I come back to the sound argument made by one of my hon. friends in connection with Holland. He pointed out that our trade with Holland was favourable to us. At the time the French treaty was broken, it was alleged that our trade with France was adverse. Figures were given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to support this contention. Just in passing, I may say that he has submitted to the trying ordeal of the last week with a spirit and intelligence which warrants my highest compliment. It was stated that on the basis of figures supplied by the Department of Trade and Commerce, our trade with France was adverse. In reply to this statement the French consul in Montreal, Mr. Marchal, published a letter in the Montreal Gazette, couched in the most polite and concise terms, showing that the trade returns as compiled by the French government gave an entirely different result than those published in Ottawa. He did not contend that the figures published here were false, not at all; he simply proved that there was a difference in the method of computation. This demonstrates once more that statistics do not always tell the truth. France figures her imports by tracing up the country of origin of goods coming into the country. Whether they come from Montreal, Quebec, Halifax or Saint John to Havre, Cherbourg or Bordeaux, or from Canada via other countries, they are all counted as Canadian goods. We figure our exports by the country of consignment; with the result that millions of dollars worth of Canadian goods are shipped to England to be reshipped to France as British goods. I do not begrudge prosperity to the British trader or broker; but I. claim for Canada the right to sell its goods to France, to Japan, to China or any other country as its own goods and to reap the full benefit of trade and international comity by being able to demonstrate, as in the case of France, that we have shipped more goods than are shown by our figures. I hope this matter will be adjusted

Mr. Speaker, I
have only a few words to add to what I said before recess. There are two economic groups; first, the consumers. One cannot look at a table such as that which I put on Hansard before six o'clock showing the degree of protection accorded the textile manufacturers, without realizing that very heavy tribute is being levied upon the people of Canada. Millions of dollars extra are being paid by the people for clothing, blankets, and other necessities of life by reason of tariff protection. It seems to me it is a very important consideration whether it is worth while for the people of this country to pay such a heavy tribute to a particular industry. Turning from the group of people whom we commonly call the consumers-I suppose we are all consumers-to the class engaged in the production of these commodities, it seems to me that we have to distinguish clearly between the manufacturers themselves, the owners of the factories, and their employees. We have been inclined to take it for granted that whatever was of advantage to the manufacturers would be of advantage to their employees. But this is true to only a very limited degree. It is quite possible that if very large profits were not permitted to the manufacturers they might close their doors, and temporarily a large number of employees might be thrown out of employment. On the other hand, as we tried to emphasize the other evening, it by no means follows that protection to the manufacturer is any guarantee of a decent standard of livelihood to the men engaged in the industry. Protection does not in any way guard against low standards or ensure that our own manufacturers shall not be guilty of what might truly be termed unfair competition.
I want for a moment to call attention to the article contained in the agreement which I read just before recess:
All persons who become members of or associated or affiliated with any labour organization of any kind whatsoever shall thereby entitle the company on its becoming aware of the fact to immediately discharge them without notice and to hold as forfeited all wages due them by the company at the time of such discharge notwithstanding anything in this agreement.
That is very little less than a slave pact. I should think that if our Labour department were really active in the interests of labour they would immediately take steps to protect the worker in his right to organize.
If this country were properly seized of the importance of the inherent rights of citizens it would not tolerate the use of an agreement of this kind by any company engaged in industry.

I have not the facilities for investigating it; if I went on the premises of the company I presume I would be immediately ordered off because it might be considered that I was trying to organize the employees. It is an anomaly that we should be giving special privileges to these textile companies, yet refuse to assume any responsibility with regard to the conditions which prevail in these factories. As I showed a few evenings ago, very low wages are paid; the Canada Year Book demonstrates that. So we come back to this position, that we ought to guarantee to the people engaged by these corporations the right of association, the right to decent wages and decent living conditions; and that companies failing to grant these should not be permitted to be the recipients of special privileges. That is a preeminently reasonable position. The government is in a position very readily to put such a principle into effect, notwithstanding any provisions of the British North America Act.
There is only one other matter that I should like to mention before this agreement passes. The arrangements which we are considering tend to stabilize tariffs at a very high level, and this is unsatisfactory both from the standpoint of the consumer in Canada, and from that of international relations. We, with other nations, are putting up tariff barriers that sooner or later will lead us into complications that may easily result in physical war. We are not justified in adopting such a policy, and for that reason I shall have to vote against the bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a brief statement before the vote is taken. I am voting against the treaties since in my opinion
1446	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
they stabilize the Canadian tariff at a high level, the highest it has ever reached. It is a manufacturer's tariff, in which the consumer was forgotten. I vote against the treaties since the monetary policy carried out by this government makes it impossible for the Canadian farmers to sell their goods in the British market, and in so far as they do sell any goods they lose around $1.10 on every British pound's worth of Canadian goods put upon the British market.
I will give you some quotations from actual exporters to prove the truth of that statement. The Country Guide, of November, 1932, a magazine printed in Winnipeg, carried interviews with several exporters. The initials of the interviewer are R.D.C. The first interview was with Mr, Bruce Burns, president of Burns Brothers, a firm which shipped 3,000 cattle to Great Britain this year. The interviewer asked Mr. Burns what would be the effect on cattle prices on the St. Boniface market if the pound were worth $4.86, and he answered:
If the pound were anywhere near par we could pay $20 more on the St. Boniface market for an export steer, if we were exporting. But the exchange situation has got so bad that we went out of the export business last August.
The interviewer then asked Mr. F. M. Baker, western representative of the Industrial and Development Council of Canadian Meat Packers, what he had to say in relation to bacon going on the British market.
Mr. Baker said:
The loss due to exchange alone is approximately $1.40 per 60 pounds of Wiltshire and since that amount of Wiltshire is made from 100 pounds of live hog the loss is $1.40 per 100 pounds on bacon hog.
And since a bacon hog will weigh 200 pounds, that means a loss of $2.80 on every bacon hog put on the British market, due to the monetary policy of the present government.
Then the interviewer interviewed Mr. T. J. Coyle, of T. J. Coyle and Company, dealers in butter and produce, and Mr. Coyle said at the end of quite a long paragraph:
When the pound dropped below $4.25 last August we quit exporting butter to the old country altogether.
The same man, speaking of eggs, said:
With the pound worth $4.86 the loss on sterling is eliminated, and that much added to the producer price brings it up to 18J cents.
Instead of 11 cents a dozen as they are at the moment. That is a very serious thing. There was a loss of $20 on an export animal, $2.80 on an export hog, the stopping of butter exports altogether, a loss of 7 cents a pound on turkeys and 7 cents a dozen on eggs when this interview was given.
I oppose the treaties because the present government does not provide for the free entry of any British goods into Canada. Even on goods called free, the exchange dumping duty of 18 per cent and the 3 per cent excise tax must be paid, making a protection of 21 per cent against so called free goods. Then if the Canadian farmer sells his produce in the British market at world prices and gets paid in the British pound, when he brings that pound back to Canada he gets only S3.78 for it. But if he buys British goods with that British pound this government charges him a duty based on the par value of the pound, plus the exchange dumping duty on the duty paid value plus 3 per cent excise tax. In other words, the government gets the farmer whether he brings back money or goods. Therefore, as a representative of the farmers in the House of Commons I could not possibly support such a treaty.
These treaties will adversely affect our trade with other countries against whom we have raised our intermediate tariff. In this I am giving my own opinion, but I think it is correct. There are possibly twenty of these countries, and I think in this connection we will lose much more than we will gain. Lastly, the treaties do not recognize the economic unity of the world and the right of trade to flow where it will. These treaties have set up another group of obstructions seeking to force trade into new channels. For all these reasons I must vote against the treaty now before the house.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
Since the government has taken the full responsibility for conditions as they exist, and we are not to have any commission to consider the matter further, I presume that all that any of us can now do is to lay before the house the actual conditions that prevail across Canada today, with a view to having some policy adopted which will help at least in part to alleviate the situation. How do we actually deal with the large number of people who are today unemployed? May I point out that there is a certain class of them whom we are simply getting rid of. Out of a grand total of deportations for the past year and a half of some 15,368, there were 9,446 who were deported simply because they had become public charges. I am not holding the government altogether responsible for this action because I know that there has been a good deal of pressure on the part of municipalities to have these people deported; but it is not fair that when we have invited immigrants to come to this country, people who very often have broken up their homes and given up jobs in the old land, having torn themselves loose to come here, expecting to find the opportunities which were promised to them, we should, as soon as they find themselves unable to obtain work, simply send them back to the countries from which they came. I do not think it is at all fair. In this land of plenty we should have assumed our obligations to care for them.
May I call attention to another class, those who are commonly known as transients. They are the men who had a good deal to do with the construction of our railroads, the building-up of our cities, and pioneering in the west, single men for the most part who

Unemp'oyment-Mr. Woodsworth
went wherever unskilled labour was needed. They were very often imported by contractors, being told that there would be opportunities for work in this country. Now they are regarded as the scum of the earth. No community will accept responsibility for them. I had a letter the other day from a friend of mine in Winnipeg. He writes:
Conditions here have become deplorable. The city seems to be filling up with destitute men. A man called at my house this afternoon and after feeding him I drove him down to the Water street hall for him to get a night's lodging. The place was full to the doors. I saw fully thirty men lying in their filth and rags within five feet of the doors-an abominable sight. We -always provided for our cattle better. I took the fellow to a hotel and got him a bed and intend applying for his deportation tomorrow, as he is an Englishman with two years' residence in this country and told me he had six years' service in the imperial army.
It seems to me that that is not a fair way to deal with our English immigrants, and especially with those who have served their country during the war. I have had another communication from a gentleman connected with the unemployment conference in Winnipeg. He states that a large number of transients were stranded in Winnipeg as the result of the ban by the government upon freight train riding. He writes:
As many of them as can get into the old immigration hall in the industrial bureau are allowed to sleep on the floor there at nights without beds or blankets, and those who are unable to crowd into the sleeping quarters there are compelled to go to the police station.
In the morning these boys are given a bowl of porridge each, a cup of coffee, some dry bread and a little syrup. The only other meal they receive is in the evening, when they get a bowl of thin soup, more dry bread, and a cup of coffee.
I took this matter up with Alderman Andrews, chairman of the unemployed relief committee of Winnipeg, and he advised me the city would not assume responsibility for the feeding of these transients, but from a humanitarian basis the men are given the meagre food they now receive rather than let them starve.
And again:
It is frankly admitted by some of the Winnipeg aldermen that their purpose in giving the transients such meagre food and these horrible sleeping quarters is to force them to leave town and run the risk of being jailed in some other town for a violation of the government's order prohibiting riding on freight trains.
On one occasion when I was motoring I gave one of these transients a ride. After I had driven about thirty miles he put a revolver under my nose, but I punched him in the right place.

It is possible that there are some of these transients who become 63719-82
outlaws but there are tens of thousands of them who up to very recently have been good workingmen. These men are being made into criminals, and the society which treats them in such a wretched manner is responsible. Some of this group of men of whom I spoke were assisted to come east to their homes, but protests were made by Toronto and Montreal against their coming back. They are kicked around from one place to another, no one will assume any responsibility for their welfare. I should like to quote another instance in connection with the homesteaders from the Peace River district. I received a communication with regard to this matter enclosing a letter which describes the situation and which reads in part:
-homesteaders from the Peace River district who are not allowed to return home as freight riders, the same manner as they were permitted to come to the harvest operations.
They were permitted to go in that manner and then were not allowed to return. The letter continued:
The people of Busby these days see many of the homesteaders making their homeward journey under different circumstances. A week ago fourteen men were stranded in Busby, some of whom had a club used on their hands to make them release their hold on the cars. That night some slept in the bush, some in the United church, others on the floor in the hotel. Next day four more weary and footsore arrived from Edmonton, and that night eighteen men were housed in the church. Sunday, the majority started northward by the tie route. Next day the others scattered, some homeward, others back to the city. Some of the group belonging to the district around Dawson creek, nearly five hundred miles from Edmonton. One man had seven dollars cash, two had less, etc.
And again:
The chief grievance of all these men is that they were allowed to come south freight riding and now denied that privilege to get home.
And again:
The order prohibiting freight riding is inexcusable under the existing circumstances. To say the least, the order is an act of crass stupidity.
Certain of these men have been arrested, some of them complain of having been roughly handled, and they state that at times money has been taken from them by the police without due process of law. I am not in position to investigate that accusation. These men are not to blame for the conditions which exist, they took the only means at hand to get to the places where they hoped to secure work.

I should like to deal with the conditions which exist in the relief camps. I shall read first an extract from a despatch from Ottawa _ giving a description of these camps. It reads:
_ In these camps, in which up-to-date sanitation has been installed and free medical attention will be given, food, shelter and clothing will be provided.
Opposed to that description, I have the following letter from a gentleman in Winnipeg which seems to indicate that conditions are not as described in the press:
I have been asked by a committee of men, who are working at Riding Mountain park, to bring to your attention the utterly disgraceful situation which exists there. Picture to yourself a tar paper shack 79 feet x 24 with no window's, along each side there is a row of double deck bunks, these are spaced off with 8x1 board so that there is room for two men in each bunk. The bunks are filled with straw and you crawl into them from the foot end. Along the front, of the lower bunk a narrow board is placed upon Which the men may sit. The place is very meagrely lighted and ventilation by three skylights. There are two stoves in the shack in front one of which eordwood is piled up. So narrow is the passageway between the bunks that when the men are sitting on the bench there is scarcely room to pass between them. This shack 79 x 24 houses 88 men. There is a marked resemblance to a hog pen or a dog pound. At all times the place reeks of the foul smell and at night the air is simply fetid. The floor is dirty and the end of the shack, where there is a trough where the men wash, the floor is caked with black mud. I asked several old-timers their opinion of it and they state in fact that it is without any question the worst camp they have ever seen on the American continent. The toilet is thoroughly filthy, unsanitary, and far too small.
And again:
The terrible thing about it is that many of the men who are congregated in this camp are teen aged Canadian boys forced into close association with mature men, who have tramped the streets and bummed their w'ay through the country, with the result that the outlook of

these boys stands a good chance of being completely warped and their characters so degraded and demoralized that their future is unquestionably seriously menaced.
The question may be asked:	Why do men
suffer such indignities, and four reasons are given in the letter, as follows:
1.	Fourteen miles from the nearest railway.
2.	Stool pigeons who report the least attempt at organization.
3.	Intermittent surveillance by mounted police.
4.	General breaking down of morale.
These men are said to be paid twenty cents a day and their board and are working on the completion of an eighteen hole golf course.

The hon. gentleman is
entirely wrong in his statement. That camp is located in my constituency and I take exception to his remarks. That letter is absolutely wrong. Those men are taken in and used in the very best way. Their camp is far better than the one at Camp Hughes and the other camps in western Canada. Those men are well treated.

I hope that what the hon. gentleman has said may be correct, but I say that the letter from which I have read from a man who I believe thinks he is telling me the truth, and this is another condition which ought to be investigated.
