speechtext:
My answer to that question is one which I think the hon. gentleman himself will appreciate on reflection. The
Unemployment-Mr. Bennett

War Measures Act was then in force, and when I endeavoured to suggest that we should deal with the problem as one of peace, order and good government, which would bring it within the jurisdiction of this government, I was met with opposition such as will be within the memory of the house. We did succeed in securing the legislation for a limited time, but one does not like to face that sort of thing merely for the purpose of having the House of Commons sit for a month without obtaining results. With the aid of the provinces it would be competent for this parliament to enact appropriate legislation; that was done under the War Measures Act. That act now has ceased to have effect, and the condition to which the hon. gentleman has referred is a condition that no longer exists. I repeat that at the moment there is no authority on the part of this government or this parliament to appoint and clothe with appropriate powers a federal relief commission. We have done this: A representative of the Department of Labour has visited the four western provinces, and with them he has gone into this matter. They have appointed their own commissions, by means of which they are endeavouring to discharge their obligations, and the minister is giving them such assistance as may be necessary in the premises. We must realize that there are provinces in this confederation that will not tolerate the dominion interfering with or endeavouring to trench upon their jurisdiction; that they have made quite clear, and therefore any attempt on our part to create a federal unemployment or federal relief commission not only would be beyond our power but would be met at once with the resistance which any interference or trenching upon the jurisdiction of the provinces would involve.
I apologize, Mr. Speaker, for taking longer than I had expected in making this statement. I cannot promise that the legislation I mentioned in my speech of April 29, 1931, will be forthcoming, but I can promise that it will be no fault of ours if we do not meet with the provinces between now and January 30 next, and at least arrive at some conclusion with respect to those controversial matters which must be settled before any appropriate action can be taken by this parliament.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I am sure the
minds of hon. gentlemen on both sides of the house will be greatly relieved at the statement which the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), made at the opening of his remarks, which was to the effect that he had no desire to curtail discussion on the all-important ques-
tion of unemployment relief. My right hon. friend could hardly be surprised if not only those on this side of the house but the country generally gathered from what he said yesterday that such was the purpose of the administration in seeking to avoid discussion of the amendment which had been moved' and which was before the house. May I say also that that impression was made doubly strong by the ruling of his honour the Speaker and by the arguments by which the ruling was supported. The impression certainly did exist very generally that this House of Commons was not to have an opportunity to discuss further or at any considerable length the question of unemployment or unemployment relief. I am not surprised that the Prime Minister came very quickly to recognize how serious would be the consequence of a step of the kind on the part of the administration. As I gather now from the Prime Minister's remarks, the house is free to discuss, on going into committee of ways and means, or on going into committee of supply, any grievance which it may wish to bring to the attention of the administration, and to do so in pursuance of the rights which we have all along assumed and claimed belonged to the House of Commons at any time the government was asking it to consider ways and means or supply.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I am also pleased to find myself very largely in agreement with much that the right hon. the Prime Minister has said this evening, both as to the position of this parliament in dealing with the question of unemployment, and as to the government's intention with respect to certain legislation which I understand, it now hopes may be enacted by parliament at some subsequent session. But may I say to the Prime Minister that, if anyone is responsible for a wrong impression having been created as to the powers and duties of this parliament with respect to the relief of unemployment, that person is the right hon. gentleman himself. The position stated by the Prime Minister this evening in relation to the rights, duties and responsibilities of municipalities, provinces and the dominion with respect to unemployment relief, was the position which wras taken by myself as leader of the government when we were in office. We took the position, which had been taken by a previous administration, namely, that unemployment relief was in the first instance, the responsibility of the municipality; that it became, next, the responsibility of the provinces; and that it was only when one or more of the provinces found themselves unable to cope

Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
with the problem of unemployment that it became a national emergency involving an obligation on the part of the federal government to assist the provinces in meeting the situation. That was the position which we took and maintained.
Hon. gentlemen opposite, however, know full well that, when they were sitting on this side of the house, in the two sessions immediately preceding the last general election, they consistently opposed that position, and no one more so than the present Prime Minister. He denounced us for taking an attitude of the kind, stating that it was an obligation of the federal administration. My right hon. friend not only adopted that attitude in parliament at the time, but, when an appeal was made to the country in a general election and the government of the day sought consistently to maintain in the country the position which it had taken in this house, he led an attack against the then administration on the ground that unemployment was a national obligation, and that the government in asserting the position it had taken, was seeking to evade its responsibility. May I here remind my right hon. friend how often in the course of that campaign, he said, "Mr. King promises you conferences; I promise to end unemployment."
We have heard a good deal from my right hon. friend this evening about conferences. This comes two years or more after the time at which a conference of the kind to which he refers tonight would have been held by a Liberal administration, had it been in office. No one was more emphatic throughout the last campaign than my right hon. friend in stating that the then existing condition constituted a national emergency. It was he who, over and over again in his speeches in different parts of the country, sought to arouse the people to a belief that the federal government was not doing its duty in not so regarding the situation. As my right hon. friend himself will remember, he made frequent references to the sufferings of the poor, the cries of the needy. Time and again he said that if I could not hear them, he at least could and that he would find means whereby those cries would be heard in parliament. That was the position he took at that time. It was not that the poor we have always with us. That was not what he said when appealing to the electorate. He told them in unmistakable terms that it was the duty of the federal government to see that every man who wished to work should have work. He repeatedly told the people that if he were returned to power, they would have work-work, not doles.
I have no desire at the present time to go back over the past. If the seriousness of the unemployment situation today has at least brought-
Oh, oh.

Will the hon. member who persists in perpetually interrupting please try to keep quiet when we are discussing so serious a matter as this, and when I am doing my best, in the grave circumstances at present existing to be as nearly in agreement with the Prime Minister as I can.
The right hon. gentleman himself interrupts as much as anyone in this house.
Sit down.
The right hon. gentleman interrupts himself.
Sit down.

I have been unable to hear what the hon. member who has just spoken has said, but, inasmuch as I did not mention any hon. gentleman in particular, be evidently takes the remark as applying to himself. When the Prime Minister comes forward, two years and a quarter after we asked him to take the step which he now says he is about to take, and I seek to agree with him, I hope that hon. members will at least give me a chance to show wherein, so far as it is possible so to do, this side of the house will endeavour to work in cooperation with the administration. This country is confronted at the present time with a situation more serious, so far as unemployment is concerned, than it has had to face in the whole of its history. I realize that the government has a very difficult situation confronting it, and that it is finding it extremely hard to cope with that situation. As I have said, I do not wish to go over the past, beyond making perfectly clear what our position has always been. In do particular have we changed our position.
I wish further to make clear wherein the present condition so far as it has to do with state aid has come to be what it is at the moment, namely, that of the great body of the people looking to the federal government for the solution of its problems. The Prime Minister himself, more than any one else, has encouraged the people in that point of view. He did so until the moment he came into office, and for the first and second session afterwards, and he must not be surprised if, at the present time, some of the people still continue to believe that he meant something at least of what he said. May I remind the
145S	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
house that at the special session of 1930, called to deal with the problem of unemployment, I advocated very strongly the immediate calling of a dominion-provincial conference to discuss the very questions referred to this evening by the right hon. the Prime Minister. I pointed out that there were many social services which were being undertaken by the provinces, some of which, I thought, could, to the advantage of Canada as a whole, be taken over by the federal administration and made a matter of federal concern. I pointed out also that there was need for consideration of the financial arrangements between the provinces and the dominion, and their revision, and I begged hon. gentlemen opposite not to continue without further consideration their grants in aid to the provinces for one purpose or another until this conference had been called.
I am sure the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) remembers that when, in the session of 1931, he brought in his measure to renew the period for a grant in aid to technical education, I said to him that I thought it would be wiser for the administration to hold that measure over until after a conference of this kind had taken place, and there was a more definite understanding as to what amounts the provinces were to receive from the federal treasury, and knowledge of the respective positions of the dominion and the provinces with regard to these matters. But my hon. friend the Minister of Justice persisted in putting through his measure, and hon. gentlemen opposite supported him. What has been the result? Although the measure is on the statute books, no contributions have as yet been made under its provisions. The government has violated its own act. As I understand, no contributions have been made to the provinces under this act notwithstanding the fact that the statute itself says that they should be made.
That is only one instance, but I cited many others where grants in aid were being made to the provinces from the federal treasury for different purposes, and advocated that, inasmuch as the situation was serious, as those who could see at all must have known, it was desirable to bring about such a conference forthwith.
I am gratified that the Prime Minister has tonight announced that it is at last the intention of the government to take such a step. May I add that I urged him to take that step, not only at the special session, but at the session of 1931, and again this spring at the session of 1932. It is gratifying to know that the government has come to see the wisdom of the course urged upon them from

this side of the house over two years ago. It comes a little late, but it is better late than never, and I, for one, sincerely hope that, when the conference does take place, some of the aims which have been mentioned here tonight may in a large part be realized.
My right hon. friend has spoken of unemployment insurance and has touched upon the question of jurisdiction. Here again there is in more particulars than one no difference between the point of view presented tonight by the Prime Minister and that presented on previous occasions by those who sit on this side. We have always recognized that, if there was to be a national scheme of unemployment insurance, or a national scheme to deal with any phase of social insurance, it would have to be by agreement between the provinces and the dominion, or possibly by an amendment to the British North America Act which could be made as a result of such agreement. Taking that view, we advocated two years and more ago that the government should then and there appoint a commission to deal with the question of unemployment and kindred matters, so that once the necessary data had been secured as a guide to the measure to be drafted, whatever steps might be necessary in the way of an amendment to the British North America Act in order to permit a national scheme of insurance to go into effect could be taken at the earliest possible moment. One can only now say that more than two years have been lost, and that, after the lapse of that time, the government has come to the position which we of the opposition urged upon them from the time they came into office. I am' glad, indeed, that the government has come around to our position. We shall I trust be able to work in harmony and cooperation with them. We commend them for their action, but at the same time, we cannot but regret that so long a period has gone by which might have been turned to good account in furthering and advancing such an all-important measure.
One of the reasons, I think, why so much time has elapsed is that my right hon. friend failed to appreciate the real significance of the depression which had come upon the world. In that again, his view at the outset was entirely different from the view entertained by those of us on this side of the house. During the campaign of 1930, I made, over and over again, the statement that unemployment was beginning to be what it was because of world conditions and that Canada was coming more and more under the shadow of that widening expanse of depression which had begun in

Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
Europe and the effects of which were beginning to be felt in all parts of the world. My right hon. friend, however, took the opposite view; he told the electors that the depression in Canada was due to a local condition, to the mistakes in policy of the government which had been in office for the eight or eight and a half years previous. Wherever he went he stressed with emphasis that the condition was luoal and temporary and would pass if he and his supporters came into office. I think they have discovered since they came into office that we had a more accurate view than they of the economic situation, that our vision was a great deal broader, clearer and truer with respect to the condition of the world elsewhere and its bearing upon conditions in Canada. I remember that at the end of the first or second session I said to my right hon. friend that he had better make up his mind as to what line he was going to pursue from then on, that he would have to decide whether he was going to continue to say that condition was a local one, or assert from then on that it was a world condition. I have noticed that ever since that time hon. gentlemen opposite have been sheltering themselves behind the statement that they are unable to cope with present conditions not because they are local, but because they are world-wide in character. If we are now agreed also on that point, so much more to the good. While I admit that there is a world condition, I wish to emphasize again that the condition so far as Canada is concerned has been intensified many times by the mistaken policies of hon. gentlemen opposite since they came into office.
In dealing with the problem of unemployment a distinction should be made between what is required to meet the present, immediate needs of those who lack food, shelter or clothing and what may be necessary in the way of legislation to meet conditions of unemployment, or rather to ensure against unemployment. It must be obvious to all that unemployment is a recurrent condition and one which under any industrial system, I would say, having regard to the causes, is apt to recur in greater or less measure, regardless of what governments or individuals may seek to do. For this reason, it is essential that the state should make some provision which will help to meet the situation with regard to the unemployed.
Before I speak on the insurance phase may I say a word or two with regard to actual existent unemployent and the necessity of providing immediate relief. The condition in Canada today is such that this federal government must assume, along with the municipalities and provinces, the obligation of helping to relieve unemployment. Apart from all else, we know more than we care to say about the financial condition of the municipalities and the provinces. The sooner all get together, municipalities, provinces and the dominion, and find out just how their finances stand and what they can afford, the better it will be for all concerned. But I say that the condition is such that this federal government must assume some share of the responsibility. I disagree with the Prime Minister when he says that the federal government cannot, under the law as it stands, appoint a commission to deal with federal relief. The federal government can do anything that it wishes to do with respect to grants which it may make, with respect to the expenditure of federal money, and I shall cite as my authority the Prime Minister himself who, time and again, has made that assertion. He has, on each occasion when the unemployment question has been discussed, harked back to some decision which was made by the late Lord Haldane and others in, I think it was, the Board of Commerce case, in respect to some fair prices measure, in which reference was made to what constituted a national emergency. I am not going to quarrel with my right hon. friend's assertion as to what may or may not be done under the constitution with respect to matters of emergency; what I say to him is that all he has stated in that connection is entirely beside the mark. When we on this side of the house have advocated the appointment of a nation-wide commission which would have to do with the administration of relief, in so far as that relief was being given through moneys taken from the federal treasury, we have been speaking entirely of a federal responsibility in regard to the expenditure of federal money, its distribution and supervision. Surely hon. gentlemen opposite will agree that, with the consent of the provinces, a federal commission could function in cooperation with the provinces in the administration of relief. That is entirely a matter of agreement. If there are provinces which do not wish anything in the way of federal assistance, they ought to be quite free to say so and if they so desire, to do without. But, in a situation such as exists in Canada today, there is not, I submit, a province that, if it were called into conference with the federal government and arrangements were made which it was believed would lead to greater care in the expenditure of public moneys which were necessary for the purpose of relief, would not welcome a chance to share jointly in some scheme which would be of service to all concerned.
WOO	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
So that there will be no mistake as to what our federal powers are, may I quote the words of my right hon. friend as given to this house as recently as October 10, just last month, when he was speaking in the debate on the address in reply to the spech from the throne. My right hon. friend, as reported on page 50 of Hansard, made this statement:
While we have power to assist by grants of money; while we have power to impose conditions in those grants, as we have done, under our constitution the administration rests with the provincial authorities, and in all the statutes we have passed we have been careful to point out that while the danger and difficulty are national the administration rests with the provinces and the municipalities, and the duty of this dominion is to lend assistance in that direction.
Note these words:
While we have power to assist by grants of money; while we have power to impose conditions in those grants.
Our conditions might well be the distribution and supervision of expenditure of federal moneys by and in accordance with recommendations of a federal commission. May I in this connection repeat a suggestion that I made when giving to the house the point of view of hon. gentlemen on this side with regard to the manner in which federal relief should be administered? Our position has been that the expenditure of federal moneys on relief should be entrusted to a commission, a non-partisan one preferably to be chosen by a representative conference of parties mostly interested or, even, as I think I stated when speaking on one occasion, a commission which the government itself would appoint, assuming responsibility for its appointees, even if they were all from one political party, but nevertheless a commission which would be charged with the supervision of federal relief and the expenditure of such moneys as came out of the federal treasury. I said that I believed if a step of the kind were taken the mere fact of there being a body of this character charged with supervising relief would go very far in bringing about uniformity in methods of administration throughout Canada, the avoidance of duplication and the effecting of great economies.
I made a concrete suggestion then, and I want to repeat it this evening. I would suggest it to the ministry as a step which even yet should be taken; should be taken this year with regard to federal moneys which are to be expended on unemployment relief for purposes other than the immediate direct relief of necessitous cases. The suggestion is

this, that the federal government work in combination with the municipalities and the provinces, undertaking to grant its share of relief, but on the condition that all money which goes from the federal treasury for purposes of relief must go to the unemployed as wages in payment for the work which they will be given to perform; that no part of the federal money shall be paid to contractors or to those furnishing supplies or used for purposes of paying for superintendence of work, for equipment, the buying of tools and the like; that the federal government see to it that moneys voted- by this parliament be placed in the hands of a body of trustees, so to speak-call them by whatever name you like-to be paid out in the manner I have indicated.
May I illustrate concretely what I mean? There has just been completed in the city of Ottawa a campaign for the raising of money for unemployment relief. The money raised in this city is to be supplemented by money from the province and also by money from the federal treasury. I believe it would lead to economy in the interests of the municipality, the province and the dominion, if the federal government said: With respect to such money as we grant, it must be used for payment of actual labour performed on relief work of one kind or another which may be undertaken by the municipality and the province. What then would happen? The provinces then, in the event of their doing provincial work, would provide supplies and the necessary superintendence. The municipalities would cooperate in the same way. They already have organization at hand for the purpose of carrying out important municipal work. It would be to their interest to keep down the expenditure or superintendence, cost of construction apart from labour cost, and cost of materials and the like. With federal money going simply to pay for the actual labour that was performed, we would be sure that every dollar that was voted by the federal government would go into the pockets of the needy, the unemployed, who were being given employment, instead of a large part of it going to pay contractors for their part of the job, to pay for the material needed to put up construction camps, buildings and the like and what is to be paid for services or superintendence and the like. A step of that kind is not only feasible but has been worked out elsewhere on this continent with very great success. It helps to bring about cooperation between different parties and interests and, as I have indicated, it serves the ends of economy as well.

Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
That, I would say, should be the method of proceeding with regard to moneys voted from the federal treasury excepting such as must go to supply immediate needs in the matter of food, fuel and shelter and clothing for those who are without any one or more or all of those. There is a distinction between the immediate necessity of assisting the destitute and those who cannot work till they are fed, and the need, almost as immediate, of giving employment to those who are out of employment but who are capable of working. I believe, wherever it is possible to have work done or relief given in the form of actual work, it is altogether desirable and preferable that this should be done. After all, there is nothing that will more demoralize the manhood of our country than for men to become recipients of doles if it is all possible for them to avoid anything of the kind through getting work and being paid for the services which they are rendering. The government should take account of that, aspect of the effect of some of its own endeavours to assist those who are in need. So much for the immediate situation.
May I point out, in coming to the question of unemployment insurance, another advantage we might have had today, had the government taken the step of appointing a commission or committee to supervise the expenditure of federal moneys, not at this time or at some time later on, 'but two or two and a quarter years ago. If a body of that kind had been appointed it would by now have collected a fund of information which would be at the disposal of the government and of parliament at this time. My right hon. friend is probably going to appoint some commission to study this whole question. I should like to know how any commission appointed now or at any subsequent time could possibly acquire information at all comparable to that which would have been acquired by a commission appointed two years ago to deal with the question of unemployment relief, and which by this time would have had full knowledge of conditions as they exist in the different industries and in all parts of this dominion. So I say that, (here again, a couple of years have been lost in carrying out a policy which, apparently, the government at the moment is beginning favourably to consider.
As to the question of jurisdiction, I do not think there will be much trouble in overcoming that difficulty, provided the government is prepared to consider a national scheme. During the summer of 1930, the Prime Minister told the people of Canada in no uncertain terms that, so far as old age pensions, which are one form of social insurance, were
concerned, they could just as readily be administered by the federal government as by the provinces, and that, if the federal government could contribute fifty per cent, it could just as well contribute 75 or 99 or 100 per cent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt, but I did not say administer just as well. The administration, is for the provinces.

I accept what my right hon. friend says. He says he does not wish to claim that the dominion could carry out the administration. After all, what is perhaps of more concern to the taxpayer than the question of administration is the cost of the contribution itself. If the federal government were about to contribute one hundred per cent of what is required to meet the cost of old age pensions and made an agreement with the provinces that it would; do so only on the understanding that that one hundred per cent would be administered by the federal government instead of by the different provincial governments, I do not think the provincial governments would very long hesitate in allowing the dominion government all that was necessary in the way of latitude to secure an amendment to the British North America Act for that purpose. So I believe, Mr. Speaker, there should be little difficulty in surmounting the question of jurisdiction. I believe the day is rapidly coming when, so far as practically all forms of social insurance are concerned, it will be recognized as in the interests of the country in every way that whatever scheme there may be should be national in its scope. A national social insurance scheme, which would take care of matters of this kind on a nation-wide scale, would be much more in the interests of the country as a whole than a series of measures carried out in different ways by each of the nine provinces, to all of which the federal government would be contributing either in whole or in part. That, I believe, covers most of the points which have been referred to by my right hon. friend tonight.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that in my remarks this evening I have shown at least a desire not to be combative and not to embarrass the administration. But I do feel that I have a right to say that the steps which are now being suggested by the government are steps which we on this side advocated two years and more ago, and have consistently ever since urged upon the administration. That much I think I am entitled to claim for this side. But having said that, may I say to my right hon. friend that, in carrying out the project which he has proposed, so far as unemployment relief and unemployment insurance are concerned,
1462	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
we on this side of the house will endeavour to cooperate with him to the utmost of our ability.
I hope that when he comes to speak, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), will indicate that the government is going to place in the hands of some body of trustees, or some committee, or some commission, call it by whatever name you please, some body of independent minded men who will give their whole time and thought to this problem, the distribution and supervision of such federal moneys as may be voted by this parliament for the purpose of unemployment relief. The Minister of Labour himself must be willing to admit that the task of dealing with unemployment relief is one which is really not of a departmental nature. It has come to be a task national in its proportions and quite beyond departmental routine. The Department of Labour was established to carry on certain services, all of which have been set forth in acts of parliament. It was never contemplated that any department of the government would deal, year in and year out, with a condition in the nature of a national emergency. It is not fair to the minister, or to his staff, or to the government, or to the country, that the minister and his departmental staff should continue to seek to cope with something which they must confess they have up to the present time been unable to deal with successfully. Having been unable successfully to meet the situation, I hope now that we are facing a winter which promises to present a problem even more difficult of solution than those of the past, the government will call to its assistance some body of experts which may be able to help it in this all-important matter of the distribution and supervision of unemployment relief from federal funds.
While I am dealing with unemployment relief, may I say to my right hon. friend and the house that there is one other question closely allied to it which I believe is a matter of equally grave concern, if not of even graver conoern, to this country, and that is the condition of agriculture in Canada at the present time. Here again I do not wish to embarrass the Prime Minister or the administration. We realize that in dealing with the question of agricultural conditions in Canada the government is facing probably the largest and the most serious industrial problem which it or any other government in Canada has been called upon to face. I need not go into the reasons which make me feel that there are aspects of the situation which are too serious even to mention in this house at this stage of the debate, but what I would say to my right

hon. friend is this, that while we have been here now for nearly two months and are about to adjourn possibly at the end of the present week, up to the present time there has been no opportunity given to the house to discuss this all-important question. Apart from that, the country has been looking forward to.some declaration of policy on the part of the administration with respect to agricultural conditions. We have heard from the Prime Minister what was done last year and the year before; we have heard from him about the special moneys that were voted for the relief of western agriculture; we have heard since about what has been done in other directions; but what the country wants to know at the present time is what is going to be done this winter? What is going to be done between now and the time parliament reassembles? That is the question which I hope my right hon. friend will answer. I realize, Mr. Speaker, that at this time I am speaking on a motion to go into committee of ways and means, and that unless some amendment which is in order is moved I shall not have another opportunity to speak until that motion is disposed of. It has been my intention if necessary to move an amendment on going into committee of ways and means which would express the views of hon. gentlemen on this side as to what they believe as respects policy the country would like to know from the ministiy, and the position which we on this side would be obliged to take should the ministry not find it possible to make some declaration. I am not going to move this amendment at the present time, but I am going to read what I have had in mind to the house, and shall say to my right hon. friend that, if he will make a statement to the effect that he himself will announce what the government's policy is and will be through this winter with respect to agricultural relief, and will give opportunity to hon. members on this side of the house to consider that policy, to discuss it so that the government may have the benefit of views from all sides, then this amendment will not be moved. Unless my right hon. friend is prepared to give some such undertaking, I feel it will be our duty at an appropriate time to make a motion on going into supply or committee of ways and means-
No bargaining.

Well, if hon.
gentlemen opposite would rather have me secure what I am seeking by an amendment to avoid placing the government in a position in which it would be obliged to be faced by an amendment which it would regard as one

Unemployment-Mr. Lawson
of want of confidence, I am quite prepared to meet their wishes in that regard. What I wish to make clear at the moment is this:
I have no desire to have the government construe a wish on our part to secure a declaration of policy as any desire to promote a motion in the nature of one of want of confidence. But, if the government has no policy with respect to farm relief and agricultural distress, and is not prepared to make a statement to the house, then we cannot let this stage of the session go by without registering our position in reference thereto.
The amendment which, in that event, I would move at a subsequent stage, would be as follows:
Whereas parliament has been in session since October 6, of the present year, and is shortly to adjourn until January 30, 1933;
And whereas, since parliament assembled the government has not made any statement of policy with respect to the relief of existing agricultural conditions;
And whereas, the position of agriculture in Canada has become increasingly deplorable and, unless relieved, will bring about a condition of distress hitherto unparalleled;
This house is of the opinion that the government should immediately announce what policy, if any, it has w'ith respect to the relief of agricultural distress, and permit full consideration of the same before parliament adjourns over the months of December and January.
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, if that motion should happen to come into your hands, that it does not relate to the past; it does not relate to any discussions which have taken place; it relates entirely to the present and to the future, to what is to be done between now and the time parliament reassembles on January 30 next. As such I hope that, if it should be necessary to move it, the amendment will be found in order. But I hope, even more, that my right hon. friend will find it possible to accord to the house, with respect to a consideration of farm relief, the relief of agricultural distress, the same latitude which he now says will be accorded with respect to the discussion of unemployment relief, and that he will go one step farther and give to the house in that discussion a clear and definite statement as to the government's policy in this all-important matter.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that the house is desirous of hearing the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), but I crave its indulgence for a few minutes, in view of the statement just made by the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Mackenzie King) with reference to those of us who sat to the left of the Speaker in 1930 and opposed what he alleges was his then policy for unemployment relief. I submit that in the statement made to the house this evening not only has the right hon. gentleman endeavoured to misrepresent the policy, as enunciated tonight by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), but he also misrepresents the position which those of us who sat to the left of the Speaker-
Order. To accuse another hon. member of misrepresentation is not parliamentary.

Mr. Speaker, I retract unreservedly the word "misrepresent." I will say that the words used by the right hon. gentleman would lead this house and the country to believe that the right hon. gentleman took in 1930 a certain position which he now takes. That I say is not the fact.
The right hon. gentleman this evening said that in 1930 he enunciated the principle that unemployment relief was primarily a municipal responsibility, then a provincial responsibility, and thirdly, under certain conditions, a federal responsibility. He also said that the right hon. Prime Minister tonight recognized that doctrine which he had propounded in 1930. So far I agTee with the doctrine as stated by him. But tonight, sir, he goes a step further, and endeavours to have this house conclude that the Prime Minister said tonight that only when the provinces were unable to cope with the situation is there responsibility upon the dominion government. That, sir, is the position which he took in 1930. That is not the position which was taken by those of us who sat to your left at that time. At that time, Mr. Speaker, it was made abundantly clear by the then leader of the opposition that we then had in Canada a national condition. The Conservative members of the house then recognized, as we now recognize, that we had a national condition, and recognizing that fact, the Prime Minister immediately called a special session of parliament and voted large sums of money to assist the provinces and the municipalities in administering unemployment relief. If, sir, any proof were required of the position taken by the right hon. leader of the opposition in 1930 other than what I have already stated, surely one need only read his speech in this house, in which he positively and absolutely refused to contribute any sum whatever to any Tory province.
The right hon. gentleman tonight, with pious words and with great lamentation, regrets that this government has allowed two years to go by since it has been in power without bringing in an unemployment insurance measure. May I point out that the right hon. gentleman allowed nine years to go by while he was in
Unemployment-Mr. Gordon

power, although unemployment insurance was a plank in the Liberal platform of 1919. So far as I am concerned, sir, and those excellent labouring people whom I represent in this house, I do not propose to allow our position in 1930 or today to be understood from words used by the right hon. leader of the opposition to be other than what it is. So far as we are concerned, we recognized in 1930 and we recognize today that the conditions with which we were confronted were largely world conditions. But we also realized, as I stated during the election in 1930, and as I state here again tonight, that had it not been for the Liberal policies in this country for nine years preceding 1930, our local condition, to which the right hon. gentleman now refers, would be much better than it is today.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour) :
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will avoid tonight,
and at any future time if possible, getting into any discussion with the economists in this chamber. I do not think I could add anything to their knowledge, nor do I think the advancement of any of my views would be understood by them. Therefore in the observations I have to make I shall endeavour to confine myself to those matters of administration that for the moment are under my guidance in the Department of Labour.
I assume that I do not need to tell this house that so far as the federal end is concerned, if I may so describe it, of the relief afforded those in need in Canada, that portion has been administered through the Department of Labour,. with such additional staff as has been found necessary in order that the efforts of those primarily responsible may be rendered more effective. I offer my thanks to the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), for his kindly and magnanimous suggestion with respect to the setting up of a federal commission to follow the course of the moneys which the dominion government may subscribe to the provinces and through them to the municipalities, but I hazard the suggestion that if the right hon. gentleman will give a little more thought to the plan it will become more and more apparent that by the adoption of such a course the overlapping to which he has made reference will be accentuated rather than reduced. I have a good deal of faith in the municipal councils, the provincial administrations and the voluntary charitable organizations of this dominion. The men who comprise those bodies are elected to the positions they hold; they are just as good Canadians, probably, as the right hon. leader of the opposition and myself. I do not say this in any critical 
sense, 'but they understand their responsibilities very clearly. This dominion is so wide and offers so many complexities with respect to its domestic management, if I may so term it, that I am convinced we cannot do better than continue as we have carried on in the past and allow the intimate administration of the relief measures to be carried out under the supervision of those upon whom the primary responsibility falls, those who have to answer to their immediate communities for the success or failure of their efforts. There is, however, a measure of protection, perhaps of control and of the giving of sound advice exercised by the Department of Labour, by reason of the information at hand in the department which probably is not available to the municipalities and the provinces. That advice is being given constantly to those administering relief throughout the Dominion of Canada.
At this juncture, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make this observation: I always listen with a great deal of attention and interest to the speeches of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). Someone says it is a waste of time and thought, but I do not so consider it. A review of the pages of Hansard, however, from the first year the hon. gentleman graced this chamber, will show that in every pronouncement he has made, the phraseology is nearly always the same, he voices almost the same fears, the same suspicions, the same lack of confidence in any other human being in the world but himself, and always with patient regularity he sets up something that never resolves itself into fact. In my view that sort of declamation does not advance his position one iota. Again, there is the persistent reading of such documents as hon. members heard this evening. I am almost convinced that if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had taken the opportunity to go from coast to coast investigating camp conditions, he would have fought shy of ninety-five per cent or even ninety-nine per cent of the camps in order to pick out one where perhaps the administration was not what it should be, so that he might condemn the whole effort of every other Canadian interested in this matter, During the course of my efforts, such as they have been, in directing the expenditure of federal moneys and endeavouring to assist the provinces and municipalities in the careful expenditure of their moneys, I have made it my business on many occasions to visit these very camps, though I have not had very much time to spare. I did not see any evidence of the squalor or the disorganized effort to which reference has been made. On the

Unemployment-Mr. Gordon
contrary, I saw many hundreds of single men in those camps, happy indeed during this time of stress, which I hope will not be prolonged, to have an opportunity of working out the relief given them by the state, the municipalities, the provinces and the dominion, which really means the relief granted to them by levying tribute upon their fellow Canadians who are engaged in some kind of productive work.
It is quite true that I should like to see, as every member in this chamber would like to see, men in all walks of life guaranteed happy, productive employment. That never has been the case if I read history correctly, and I doubt if it ever will come to pass; there is always a percentage that cannot realize that sort of thing. But I do say this, that under the arrangements now made and in operation throughout the provinces of Canada, there is no reason today why any person in the dominion should go without food, without clothing, without fuel and without shelter, because the municipalities are bearing their share of the burden and bearing it manfully. The province is assuming its proper place, and so far as this dominion is concerned, while I am just as sure as I am standing here that there will be no such demand made upon it, yet if it became necessary in the last analysis, every available dollar would be directed towards seeing that the distress was relieved.
Now let us see what has been done since the first relief measures were introduced and passed by this house-and I will ask the house to pardon me if I stay fairly closely to the notes I have here, because there are a great many figures in this. The Unemployment Relief Act of 1930, which came into effect in September of that year, covered expenditures for the carrying-out of public works and the giving to direct relief to relieve unemployment until August, 1931. Under the provisions of the 1930 act, the Dominion government contributed $14,396,956.79 to public works, and to direct relief, $3,556,928.47. The total cost of administration was $43,061.97. The total expenditures under the 1930 act by the Dominion government were $17,996,947.23. This expenditure resulted in public and other works being carried out to the exent of approximately $69,000,000, including the contributions of provinces and municipalities. The direct relief expenditures by the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities totalled about $11,000,000. The carrying out of the work under the provisions of the 1930 act afforded work to 337,633 individuals for varying periods, the amount of work thus afforded 53719-93
being 7,481,449 man-days. In August of the following year, 1931, the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act of 1931 became effective, and contributions were made for the relief of unemployment under this act until the 1st day of March, 1932, and under the continuance act of 1932 operations under the 1931 act were continued until the first of May, 1932. Under the 1931 act the Dominion government agreed to contribute the sum of $35,739,312.19 towards the carrying on of works by the provinces, municipalities and the federal departments for the relief of unemployment, the total cost of such works being approximately $81,000,000. Some of this work was not finished at the expiration of the agreements on May 1, 1932. Extensions of time were arranged to different dates, extending to the fall of 1932, the gross cost of the works thus extended being approximately $14,778,000. For direct relief, the expenditures of the Dominion government, under the 1931 act, to date, amount to $11,536,789.73, which includes $5,250,000 to the Saskatchewan relief commission. Under the 1931 act the expenditures for public works gave employment to 579,024 individuals to the end of September, 1932, the total wages paid being $38,802,101.63, and a total of 13,152,384 man-days work being afforded.
After a survey of employment conditions in the shops of the Canadian National Railways, it was decided to maintain operations so as to permit of intermittent employment being given to a large number of employees. In the month of September, 1931 the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was compelled, as you all know, to shut down its shops and the former workers of these shops were without employment, concerning whom applications were made to the government for assistance. The government arranged, as has been already stated in this house, with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to open its shops on November 17, 1931, and to keep them open until December 31, of the same year, the government paying the wages of the workers employed in the shops, the railway company, however, to reimburse the government for expenditures so made. The total number of railway shop employees thus given employment was 8,455, the wages involved being $1,447,222. The cost of administration under the 1931 legislation was $84,487.57.
In the spring of this year, 1932, it became apparent to the municipalities throughout the dominion, and to the provinces, that the projection of works by the municipalities and by the provinces themselves was rapidly becoming so great a burden that the municipalities and probably the provinces would soon be

Unemployment-Mr. Gordon

impoverished and unable to carry that burden further. Intimation of this condition was made to the government by various communications, and following the custom that had prevailed from the beginning of the tenure of office of this administration, no time was lost in inviting the premiers of the various provinces to come to Ottawa in order that they might sit in conference with this government to see what steps could be taken, or what other course could be adopted so that people should not suffer for lack of the necessities of life in this country, and at the same time to try to inaugurate a plan that was within the financial competence of those concerned. As a result of that invitation, on the 9th of April last, I believe it was, that conference convened in this city. All the provinces of Canada were represented, and a general and prolonged discussion took place with respect to all the various matters and the complexities of the position as it faced those interested. It was the unanimous view of the representatives of all the provinces that they could no longer finanoe works and undertakings on the same scale that had obtained in the year prior to that date. These representations were heard by this government, and further representation was made by the provincial premiers, headed, I think I am not unfair in saying, by the premier of the province of Quebec, for whom I have the utmost and profoundest respect. He made it very clear, and he was supported in his contention by the other provinces, that he wished to promote the scheme of direct relief. Obviously the expenses to those concerned would be materially reduced. Just as soon as the scheme of direct relief could be perfected, it was put into motion, save for the completion of works which had been commenced, the stoppage of which would have resulted in a total or partial loss of the benefit of the work done. Appropriate action was taken by the Dominion government to seek the advice of the provinces as to what works should be completed, and agreements were made and understandings arrived at in this connection. Many of these works have not yet been completed; others have been.
The relief act of 1932 received assent on May 13, 1932. Under this act agreements have been completed with all the provinces except Prince Edward Island providing for a dominion non-recoverable expenditure of one-third of an amount not to exceed $600 per family for the purpose of providing a measure of self-sustaining relief to families who would otherwise be in receipt of direct relief. This scheme was to provide for the placing of such families upon the land, the

remaining two-thirds of the expenditure to be contributed by the province and municipality concerned. Agreements have been completed with respect to this project with Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia, and provide for a total dominion expenditure of $1,385,675. It may be said by some that that is a huge sum of money to be devoted to the endeavour to place some of our citizens upon the land where they can become self-supporting, but I do not think it is. This is not a colonization scheme, state-aided; it is not offered as a solution for unemployment; it is a measure which I believe to be constructive whereby selected families with agricultural background are placed upon the land where they can sustain themselves and get into some productive vocation. These families would have received at least the amount of our subscription to this scheme under direct relief.
Let me point out to the house something which I think is often overlooked. During the period from 1919 to March 31, 1932, this Dominion spent in its immigration department the sum of $36,718,454.97. That expenditure had nothing to do with the soldier settlement scheme, the three thousand family scheme or the New Brunswick five hundred scheme; that is simply the amount spent by this dominion in order to induce, invite and encourage anybody from anywhere to come to this country. Hon. gentlemen opposite may say; Oh, well, we are not all to blame because others on this side of the house, when the positions were reversed, advocated the same thing. I have searched the records and I find that when hon. members on this side were in opposition they advocated the encouraging of people to come and settle upon our lands to consolidate those lands which were served by the railways of Canada. So far as I have been able to learn they never advanced the idea that the people who were to be encouraged to come here should be other than those who were ready, willing and able to take up farm settlement along the lines of our then projected transportation system. Anyone who cares to survey the immigration into this country during the period I have mentioned will find that there was no hope of any considerable percentage of those immigrants ever taking up land and being out of competition with the industrial workers in our cities. That fact is borne out by what has happened. Go through our industrial centres, go through our lumber camps and our mines and you will see there the men who were encouraged to come to this country by the booking agents in

Unemployment-Mr. Gordon
Europe, by the steamship lines and by the iniquitous system of permits which was in vogue for a few years, displacing Canadian labour-they are not on our farms at all.
One of the first duties which this administration had to face when it came into office was to see that that condition of affairs no longer should prevail, and, as hon. members of this house now know, prompt action was taken to revise the regulations with respect to immigration into Canada. In passing let me say that very large numbers of the immigrants to whom I have referred are good workmen. The first criticism I have to make is that they are not on our lands, they are in our industrial centres; my next criticism is that their coming here was not so regulated that we could at least exclude the major portion of those who are today the instrument contributing largely to the sentiment growing up in Canada condemning their compatriots who are trying to make good.
I should like to pursue this matter a little further. We had to take measures to correct this situation. I find by reference to the figures that in the fiscal years ending March 31, we encouraged the following numbers of immigrants to come into this country:

Perhaps that last figure will require an explanation. When, in August, 1930, I came first into contact, as the responsible minister, with the Immigration department, having this situation under review and desiring if I could, without being unjust and unfair to those who had perhaps started to come to Canada and had broken connections with the old land or the land of their birth, I inquired as to how many would probably still be on their way or be covered by permits, and it was most difficult even to make an estimate of how many there were. For some reason or another the early spring of 1930 was a prolific season for permits and a great number of people whose permits had not expired because they were for five months, came forward after this government came into power. It would be obviously unjust were this government to say:	You must not and shall not
enter Canada. They had been granted the right to do so, and I think we did only what was fair and just in permitting them to come. But in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1932, immigration to Canada dropped to 25,752. Many of those are the wives and children 53719-931
under eighteen years of age of men who had come forward preceding their families, and in each case I gave very strict instructions that the settlement arrangements must be of such a kind and character that the man in this country would be able to receive and care for his dependents.
Having in mind what I have just said, and the amount of money that has been spent in those few years in the Immigration department, I think hon. members will all agree with me that the principle involved in the allocation of $1,385,675 for the purpose of carrying on from a federal standpoint what I believe has not before been attempted with the exception of the soldier settlement, is a proper one, namely, that if any Canadian money is to be spent for these purposes it should be devoted to colonization at home: until we have by a proper corrective process^ remedied to some extent the urban and rural complexion of our population, which complexion is today, as I say, most disproportionate. Only forty-five or fifty years ago our urban population was only 18 per cent; today it is almost 54 per cent of our total population. The reason is obvious.	;
The reason is obvious-the tariff policy.

speechtext:

the tariff. The tariff has been blamed for so many things and the resort to the tariff in times of stress by hon. gentlemen opposite is so frequent that I could almost put the word to music.
There were, of course, contributing causes. Industry attracted the young men and some young women from the rural to the urban districts. They were attracted undoubtedly by high wages and other considerations regarded as inducements to take up urban life. At any rate, this money has been allocated for the purpose to which I have made reference.
Prior to this step being taken I had an interview in November, 1930, after some correspondence, with the presidents of the two railway companies, Mr. Beatty and Sir Henry Thornton. In answer to a joint letter directed to me by the presidents of the two railway companies, in which they rather urged a continuance of the railways agreement in a modified and restrictive form, I directed this letter to each of them. Perhaps I may be pardoned if I read it. This one is dated October 30, 1931, and is addressed to Mr. Beatty; a similar letter was sent to Sir Henry Thornton:
I have received the joint communication of October 1st from Sir Henry Thornton and yourself, giving a review of the colonization

Unemployment-Mr. Gordon
activities of the two railways for the past five years and submitting your views with respect to an immigration and colonization program for 1931. I thank you for this letter and have to state that illness which has confined me to my room for several days has prevented an earlier acknowledgment.
We have a common purpose I trust when considering a colonization policy for this country, namely, to do that which is best for Canada both socially and industrially, giving these terms their widest construction, always bearing in mind that this is a British country with two major peoples, English and French speaking. We may differ in points regarding such policy but there is no ground for difference regarding the desired objective. I wish to state further that the conduct of immigration and colonization as a national business function must take proper cognizance of the importance of our Canadian transportation systems, particularly in view of their bearing on our whole financial and economic structure. I will not dwell on the soundness of the railways' policy as stated in your letter, namely that of projecting railways in advance of settlement. You have made it abundantly clear, both in previous public utterances and in your letter of the 1st instant, that actual and sound land settlement from a purely business point of view (as well as from the national standpoint) results in the type of business that is best for the railways, namely, the production of freight traffic, which I understand constitutes approximately 70 per cent of the total earnings of the railways. Colonization of this character conforms to my own view.
We have just concluded an emergency session of parliament, summoned to cope with a national unemployment problem. When parliament met in September it was reported on the basis of the most accurate survey and information available that 117,000 people in Canada were unemployed and that this number would be increased to 200,000 by the end of the calendar year. As Minister of Immigration and Colonization, it was my duty to analyse the situation with respect to the bearing that immigration had on the problem in hand. Analysis showed that of the total immigration of 221,561 people admitted to Canada in the sixteen months ending with July 31st of this year no less than 99,367 were males over eighteen years of age, and of this latter number 25,305 had entered in the first four months of the present fiscal year. It is clear, therefore, beyond peradventure that either substantial numbers of immigrants who have recently arrived in Canada are in the ranks of the unemployed, or conversely, they have displaced Canadians who are now unemployed.
Confronted *with this situation I could choose one of two positions-blame the immigration policy of the previous administration, including the Continental Railways agreement under which very substantial numbers of immigrants were brought to Canada in recent months; or address myself (in so far as it is my duty as Minister of Immigration and Colonization so to do) seriously to the task of assimilation and absorption of these people. I have chosen the latter course, and it is my view that Canada is now faced -with a colonization and assimilation problem of major importance within her own boundaries, and she will have little time to devote in the immediate future to the question
IMr. Gordon]
of active solicitation looking to the entry of any substantial number of people now resident in other countries. Unqualified expressions from responsible representatives in several of the provinces amply support this opinion.
It is my view that, confronted as we are with this assimilation and colonization problem within Canada, there is ample scope for constructive colonization work on the part of the railways, provinces, and the Dominion Department of Immigration and Colonization-work of a character that while primarily putting people into productive enterprise, will at the same time result in the type of colonization and settlement which your letter of October 1st so clearly points out as such sound business from the point of view of the railways. I may say that at the present time I am giving careful study to a submission from one of the western provinces which outlines a comprehensive colonization plan for settlement on the land of Canadian residents. This particular plan appeals to me as eminently constructive, and in fact for some years past I have held the view that there was a sound field within our own borders where the activities of all concerned in this great problem could in a large measure be usefully employed.
In this letter I am not attempting to reply in detail to the various points raised in your letter of October 1st. In view of the general position I have outlined I do not see that any good purpose is to be served at this juncture by attempting to fix responsibility for mistakes that have occurred, and we must all try to learn aright and apply with courage the lessons pictured by the mistakes of the past without dwelling unduly on the question as to whether these mistakes yvere made by the government, the railways, or both. Your letter, from your point of view, points out that the immigration and colonization activities of the railways have been conducted in a manner resulting only in actual placement and land settlement. I have carefully noted your reference to the issue of . "government permits" by the previous administration. I may state that as long as I am Minister of Immigration and Colonization I will take full responsibility for the number of such "permits" it will be my duty to issue. Making due allowance for the "permits" issued in 1929, and up to July 31st of the current year, together with the commitments of my predecessors, I hope that the railways will assume responsibility with respect to immigrants they have brought in or may bring in to Canada.
With regard to your recommendations, I may say that as far as assisted immigration from the British Isles is concerned we are in agreement that assistance shall continue for juvenile immigrants. For agricultural families I think passage assistance should be limited to British families coming under the New Brunswick Scheme, or any similar scheme for families, as well as the wives and children under eighteen years, of men already settled on the land.
The assistance for juvenile immigrants and the New Brunswick Scheme have since been discontinued. The letter continues:
With respect to female domestics, my view is that having regard to existing conditions, passage assistance should be discontinued for the coming year.	,
I suggest that immigration from the Continent should be limited for the time being to

those classes admissible under P.C. 183 as amended on the 14th of August last. Existing conditions indicate that we will have next year an ample supply of farm labour and I suggest no encouragement can be offered to a movement even of agricultural families who are without sufficient funds to begin farming on their own account. I am of the opinion that our inquiries into family settlement, both British and continental, will show that many of the families who came in last year and this year have drifted away from the farms either through lack of capital or because of insufficient wages. Until this condition clears up I am convinced that our immigration, particularly from the continent of Europe, must, in the interests of Canada as well as of the immigrants themselves, be limited to those agricultural families who have sufficient capital to establish and maintain themselves on the land.
In conclusion, it is very gratifying to find that you are of the same opinion as myself with reference to directing our joint efforts toward promoting British immigration in preference to any other.	_
As suggested by you, I should like very much to have a full discussion of the situation with Sir Henry Thornton and yourself here in Ottawa at a date mutually convenient.
